design_detail: Cochrane systematic review with meta-analysis (third version, pub3, of review CD001867; protocol published 1999, first version 2000, previous update 2005; this update with new authors, new searches and changed conclusions, dated 8 October 2010) of double-blind randomised controlled trials of opioid antagonists (oral or extended-release injectable naltrexone; oral nalmefene), alone or combined with other medicines, against placebo or an active control, in adults with DSM or ICD alcohol dependence, with at least four weeks of daily treatment. RevMan 5; random-effects pooling (Mantel-Haenszel risk ratios and risk differences, inverse-variance mean differences); end-of-treatment values only. Searches to January 2010. 50 trials (47 naltrexone, 3 nalmefene; 7793 participants) included; any single pooled efficacy estimate uses at most 28 trials and 4693 participants, and three included trials contributed no data.
can_establish: The average end-of-treatment difference between naltrexone (as given in the trials, mostly 50 mg a day by mouth for about 12 weeks on top of psychosocial treatment) and placebo in the proportion of detoxified, treatment-seeking outpatients with alcohol dependence who returned to heavy drinking or to any drinking, in drinking frequency, amount and GGT, and in side effects, across the double-blind trials published or made available to the reviewers by January 2010.
cannot_establish: Whether naltrexone helps people who are not treatment-seeking, not detoxified, without psychosocial treatment (given in all but two trials) or with psychiatric comorbidity or other drug use (excluded from most trials); whether benefit lasts after treatment stops (post-treatment data from at most 5 trials); whether as-needed (targeted) dosing works (excluded by design); whether injectable naltrexone or nalmefene works or how naltrexone compares with acamprosate or other medicines (2 to 4, 3 and 1 to 3 small trials respectively); and why results differ so much between trials (heterogeneity was not investigated).

sample.recruitment: Search of CENTRAL (The Cochrane Library issue 2, 2010, which holds the Cochrane Drugs and Alcohol Group register), MEDLINE (1966 to January 2010), EMBASE (1988 to January 2010) and CINAHL (1982 to January 2010) without language, date or other limits, four trial and results registers, contact with principal investigators of trials completed before 30 April 2009, key informants, sponsors and manufacturers, and reference lists (Methods › Search methods for identification of studies). The trials enrolled adults aged 18 or over with DSM-III-R, DSM-IV or ICD-10 alcohol dependence, as outpatients, mostly after detoxification with between 3 to 7 and 30 days of abstinence required before randomisation (Results › Included studies).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: double-blind RCTs with the individual as unit of randomisation, comparing opioid antagonists (any dose, route or combination) with placebo or an active control on drinking outcomes; at least four weeks of daily treatment; for post-treatment analyses at least 12 weeks of follow-up; crossover or multiphase designs only with a medication-free washout; samples with DSM alcohol abuse only if alcohol dependence made up more than 90%. Excluded at full text (44 studies, listed with reasons): open-label designs (17), single-blind designs (3), samples that were not alcohol-dependent (hazardous, heavy or problem drinking, healthy volunteers, hepatic impairment; 10), treatment shorter than 30 days, including five one-week laboratory studies (8), no control group (3), multiphase designs starting with open-label naltrexone (2) and targeted (as-needed) treatment (1, Karhuvaara 2007).
sample.demographics: Mean age 40 to 50 years in 43 trials. 40 trials enrolled both sexes with men the majority, 9 enrolled men only and 1 women only (O'Malley 2007). Most trials excluded concurrent major psychiatric disorders and other drug use; 3 trials required a psychiatric disorder (bipolar disorder; schizophrenia or schizoaffective disorder; axis I disorders) and 5 required co-occurring cocaine dependence. 14 trials were multicentre; sample sizes ranged from 20 to 1383 (COMBINE, Anton 2006), most between 80 and 200. Treatment lasted 4 to 52 weeks, 12 weeks in 34 trials; all were outpatient trials (two began with four inpatient weeks). By the editors' tally of the study tables, 32 trials were in the USA, 9 in Europe, 3 in Australia, 3 in Asia (Iran, Taiwan, Singapore) and 3 in Latin America (Brazil, Puerto Rico); the text gives 37 for the USA and lists 8 European trials (Results › Included studies).
sample.attrition: Drop-out is not an efficacy outcome here (it was moved to a moderator, a stated deviation from the protocol). For binary outcomes the review analysed everyone randomised and counted drop-outs and people lost to follow-up as having relapsed; continuous outcomes were taken as each trial reported them, whatever its handling of missing data (several trials used available-case, last-observation or completer analyses). Drop-out in the trials varied widely, from 1.4% (Krystal 2001, placebo) to 77.8% (Lee 2001, placebo) of an arm in the study tables. Pooled drop-out for any reason, naltrexone against placebo: RR 0.92 (0.83 to 1.01), 37 trials, 5572 participants (Data and analyses, Comparison 1, outcome 55).
sample.selection_effects: Treatment-seeking outpatients, almost all detoxified before randomisation and most free of psychiatric comorbidity and other drug use, receiving psychosocial treatment in all but two trials; the estimates are therefore add-on effects of medication in a selected treatment population, mostly in the USA. Studies were selected by one author, with a second consulted only in case of uncertainty. For return to any drinking, results for 7 trials (1776 of 4693 participants), including COMBINE, came from investigators rather than publications; for COMBINE the review computed the outcome from the trial data set.

exposure.measurement: The randomised intervention: naltrexone in 47 trials (oral in 43, extended-release injectable in 4) or nalmefene in 3, against placebo or an active control. Adherence was monitored by pill counts in most trials, riboflavin markers in 5, electronic bottle caps in 7, and naltrexone or 6-beta-naltrexol levels in a few. Drinking was self-reported, mostly by Timeline Follow-Back interview (39 trials), with breath, blood or urine alcohol, collateral reports, GGT or carbohydrate-deficient transferrin used to check self-reports in about 30 trials (Results › Included studies; Risk of bias in included studies).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions as the review reports them: oral naltrexone 50 mg a day in most trials, 100 mg a day in five (including COMBINE) and 150 mg a day in one (Pettinati 2008a); extended-release injectable naltrexone at four-week intervals at 150 to 400 mg; oral nalmefene 5 to 80 mg a day. Treatment lasted 4 to 52 weeks, most commonly three months. Detoxification was not required in 7 trials, and in 3 of them all participants were drinking when treatment began.
exposure.polysubstance: Most trials (42) excluded concurrent use of drugs other than alcohol and nicotine; 3 did not exclude illicit drug use and 5 required co-occurring cocaine dependence (cocaine outcomes were not analysed). Co-medication: sertraline in both arms of Oslin 2005; naltrexone combined with ondansetron (Johnson 2000) or sertraline (O'Malley 2008) compared with placebo; psychiatric medication allowed in the comorbidity trials.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable as a test condition: return to drinking is the outcome. Before randomisation most trials required between 3 to 7 and 30 days of abstinence after detoxification.

comparison.controls: Placebo in 40 two-arm naltrexone trials, the 3 nalmefene trials and the placebo arms of multi-arm trials. Active controls: acamprosate in 3 trials (Anton 2006; Kiefer 2003; Morley 2006) and aripiprazole (Martinotti 2008), nefazodone (Kranzler 2000) and topiramate (Baltieri 2008) in one trial each. Combination arms: naltrexone plus acamprosate (2 trials), plus disulfiram (Pettinati 2008b; no disulfiram comparison appears in the data table), plus ondansetron (1) and plus sertraline (1). Both arms received psychosocial treatment in all but two trials, most often cognitive behavioural (17) or motivational (10) therapy.
comparison.matching: Randomisation. Review's own judgments: sequence generation adequately described in 14 of 50 trials (36 unclear); allocation concealment adequate in 3 of 50 under the review's criterion (central randomisation and drug preparation plus sealed envelopes); blinding adequate in 21 (patients and research staff blinded and an identical placebo), with blinding integrity tested and confirmed in 6; baseline imbalance found and adjusted for in 4 trials (Results › Risk of bias in included studies).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to randomised comparisons; baseline equivalence (age, sex, baseline drinking, drinking or treatment history) was judged under other bias. The review mentions a proposed (and disputed) mu-opioid receptor gene predictor of response; it was not examined.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: As in the naltrexone arms: most trials excluded drug use other than alcohol and nicotine.

outcomes.instruments: Primary: return to heavy drinking (binary), return to any drinking (binary; the complement of continuous abstinence) and drinking days (percentage of study days). Secondary: heavy drinking days (percentage), amount consumed per drinking day in grams of alcohol, GGT in units per litre, and side effects (79 types reported, 45 pooled). Drop-out and drop-out due to adverse events were analysed as moderators. Post-treatment analyses were limited to the primary outcomes. Drinking was self-reported, mostly by Timeline Follow-Back.
outcomes.validity_norms: Exposure units: heavy drinking was in most trials 5 or more standard drinks on a drinking day or occasion for men and 4 for women; 4 trials used 6 for men; 8 trials also counted drinking on 5 or more days a week or a blood alcohol concentration above 100 mg/dl; one Brazilian trial counted more than 90 g of alcohol a week and another more than 9 standard drinks a day (its 5 to 9 drink category was recoded as heavy drinking for the review). Where trials did not state the alcohol content of a standard drink, country values from the ICAP 2003 International Drinking Guidelines were used to convert to grams. The reference group for every estimate is placebo (or the named active control). Side-effect ascertainment varied (checklists, open enquiry, SAFTEE, Hopkins Symptom Checklist, UKU, CIWA-Ar).
outcomes.operationalization: Benefit: fewer people returning to heavy or any drinking by the end of treatment, and fewer drinking or heavy-drinking days. Harm: risk differences for side effects; a side effect was treated as clinically relevant only if documented in at least three trials or more than 200 patients and significantly more frequent on the drug. No minimal clinically important difference was defined.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. 7 counts the review's outcome families for naltrexone against placebo (three primary, three secondary efficacy outcomes and side effects). The data table holds 103 pooled analyses across six comparisons (60 for naltrexone against placebo, 47 of them side effects), each tested at p of 0.05 or below.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Trial level, by the review's judgments: adequate blinding of patients and research staff with an identical placebo in 21 of 50 trials, confirmed by testing in 6; objective checks of self-reported drinking in 30 (31 in another paragraph). Review level: outcome statistics were coded independently by two authors and compared value by value; risk of bias was rated by one author and checked by a second.

analysis.effect_sizes: Naltrexone against placebo, end of treatment (random effects): return to heavy drinking RR 0.83 (95% CI 0.76 to 0.90), 28 trials, 4433 participants, tau-squared 0.02, NNTB 9.09 (6.66 to 14.28); return to any drinking RR 0.96 (0.92 to 1.00), 27 trials, 4693, I2 28%, fixed-effect sensitivity analysis RR 0.95 (0.92 to 0.98); drinking days MD -3.89 percentage points (-5.75 to -2.04), 26 trials, 3882, I2 94%, tau-squared 9.59; heavy drinking days MD -3.25 (-5.51 to -0.99), 15 trials, 1715, I2 81%, tau-squared 10.71; grams per drinking day MD -10.83 (-19.69 to -1.97), 16 trials, 1838, I2 66%; GGT MD -10.37 U/L (-18.99 to -1.75), 16 trials, 1645, I2 61%. Side effects: any RD 0.05 (0.01 to 0.09); nausea RD 0.10 (0.07 to 0.13), 25 trials; daytime sleepiness 0.09 (0.05 to 0.14); serious adverse events RD -0.02 (-0.05 to 0.00); drop-out due to adverse events RR 1.60 (1.15 to 2.23), 22 trials; drop-out for any reason RR 0.92 (0.83 to 1.01), 37 trials. Post-treatment: return to heavy drinking RR 0.86 (0.75 to 0.99), 5 trials, 1061; return to any drinking RR 0.94 (0.79 to 1.11), 2 trials, 185 (fixed effect). Funding: industry-sponsored RR 0.90 (0.78 to 1.05), 7 trials, 1121; non-profit 0.84 (0.77 to 0.91), 19 trials, 3125. Published against investigator-supplied results for any drinking: 0.94 (0.90 to 1.00), 20 trials, against 0.98 (0.92 to 1.04), 7 trials. Injectable naltrexone: any drinking RR 0.92 (0.84 to 1.00), 2 trials, 486; drinking days MD -8.54 (-15.77 to -1.31), 2 trials, 335 (fixed effect); heavy drinking days -3.05 (-8.46 to 2.35), 3 trials, 357. Naltrexone against acamprosate: heavy drinking RR 0.96 (0.87 to 1.06), any drinking 0.97 (0.91 to 1.04), 3 trials, 800. Naltrexone plus acamprosate against placebo: heavy drinking 0.71 (0.38 to 1.35), any drinking 0.70 (0.35 to 1.39), 2 trials, 694. Nalmefene against placebo: heavy drinking RR 0.85 (0.67 to 1.08), 3 trials, 396. Editors' calculations: the NNTB implies a risk difference of about 0.11 (0.07 to 0.15) for return to heavy drinking; approximate 95% prediction intervals from the printed tau-squared values (t distribution, k-2 degrees of freedom) are RR 0.61 to 1.12 for return to heavy drinking, -10.6 to 2.8 percentage points for drinking days and -10.7 to 4.2 for heavy drinking days, rough because tau-squared is printed to two decimals; a z-test of the industry and non-profit subgroup estimates gives p of about 0.43, and of published against investigator-supplied results p of about 0.31. No control-group event rates or absolute numbers of people per arm are printed outside the forest plots, which are images.
analysis.covariates: None at review level (randomised comparisons). Four trials adjusted for baseline imbalances in their own analyses.
analysis.preregistration_detail: Cochrane protocol published in Issue 3, 1999; review first published Issue 3, 2000. The section on differences between protocol and review lists: two authors added; primary and secondary outcomes re-selected during data extraction according to their availability; drop-out moved from an efficacy outcome to a moderator; tau-squared and Egger's regression test added; a sensitivity analysis by funding source added. The planned meta-regression of heterogeneity was postponed to a later version (Methods › Subgroup analysis and investigation of heterogeneity).
analysis.selective_reporting: Several comparisons are reported in the text with numbers that are not in the data table (nalmefene return to any drinking, heavy drinking days and dizziness; naltrexone plus acamprosate drinking days and GGT; naltrexone against aripiprazole, nefazodone and topiramate; naltrexone with ondansetron or sertraline), and one analysis in the data table (outcome selection bias, published against investigator-supplied results) is not described in the methods or results. Two analyses use fixed-effect models although the methods state random effects throughout. The planned investigation of heterogeneity was not done.
analysis.power: Not addressed. The primary estimates rest on 26 to 28 trials and 3882 to 4693 participants; injectable naltrexone on 2 or 3 trials (335 to 486 participants), nalmefene on 3 trials (396), each head-to-head or combination comparison on 1 to 3 trials, and post-treatment estimates on 5 trials (1061) or 2 (185).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 26 to 28 double-blind trials, mostly of oral naltrexone given for about 12 weeks with psychosocial treatment to detoxified outpatients with alcohol dependence, naltrexone reduced the proportion returning to heavy drinking (RR 0.83, 0.76 to 0.90; NNTB about 9), drinking days by about 4 percentage points, heavy drinking days by about 3 points, alcohol per drinking day by about 11 g and GGT by about 10 U/L, with large between-trial heterogeneity (I2 61 to 94% for the continuous outcomes; editors' approximate prediction interval for return to heavy drinking RR 0.61 to 1.12). It did not clearly change return to any drinking (RR 0.96, 0.92 to 1.00; significant only with a fixed-effect model). It increased gastrointestinal and sedative side effects (nausea RD 0.10) and drop-out due to adverse events (RR 1.60), without more serious adverse events. Evidence on injectable naltrexone, nalmefene, head-to-head comparisons and combinations comes from 1 to 4 small trials each, and post-treatment evidence from 5 trials.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that "Naltrexone appears to be an effective and safe strategy in alcoholism treatment", with effects described as moderate but worthwhile given limited options. Gaps: (1) the implications for practice say naltrexone helps to "support abstinence", while the review's abstinence outcome (return to any drinking) was not significant under its prespecified random-effects model; (2) the abstract and the summary of main results say injectable naltrexone missed significance, but its drinking-days result was significant (MD -8.54, -15.77 to -1.31; 2 trials, fixed effect); (3) the quality-of-evidence section says the trial design features ensure high methodological quality, while the review's own appraisal found adequate allocation concealment in 3 of 50 trials and adequate handling of missing binary data in 11 of 40; (4) the conclusions rest on '50 RCTs with 7793 patients', while the headline estimate uses 28 trials and 4433 participants and three included trials contributed no data; (5) the discussion says effects fade after treatment by comparing estimates from different sets of trials (28 during treatment, 5 after), and says benefit for patients who take naltrexone regularly is likely larger than in the trials, without a per-protocol analysis; (6) the plain language summary turns the NNTB for one outcome into 'one out of nine patients was helped'; (7) the drop from RR 0.64 in the 2005 version to 0.83 is called marginal. Against this, the abstract reports the null abstinence result and the sponsorship and publication-bias analyses, and the authors say plainly that the effects are add-on benefits over psychosocial treatment and that opioid antagonists are no cure.

timeline.event: Volpicelli et al. and O'Malley et al., the first placebo-controlled trials of naltrexone in alcohol dependence (Tier B of the alcohol list), both included in this review.
First version of this Cochrane review (Srisurapanont and Jarusuraisin, Issue 3, 2000), from a protocol published in Issue 3, 1999.
Bouza et al., meta-analysis for the Spanish health technology assessment agency, cited here as finding NNTB 9 for heavy drinking and no significant effect on abstinence.

Previous update of this review (Srisurapanont and Jarusuraisin, Issue 1, 2005), cited here with RR 0.64 (0.51 to 0.82) for return to heavy drinking from 7 trials (822 patients) and 0.91 (0.81 to 1.02) for any drinking from 10 trials (1014).
COMBINE (Anton et al., 2006), the largest included trial (1383 participants); the review computed return to any drinking from its data set.
Rösner, Leucht, Lehert and Soyka, meta-analysis of naltrexone and acamprosate using unreported outcomes, by three authors of this review; cited here as agreeing with it.

This update: 50 trials; conclusions changed from the 2005 version; nalmefene trials sponsored by Lundbeck (SENSE, ESENSE1/2) and injectable naltrexone trials sponsored by Alkermes listed as ongoing and not included.

Mann et al., ESENSE 1, randomised trial of as-needed nalmefene (alcohol list Tier B, item 70; not read), one of the trials listed here as ongoing and of a regimen this review excluded by design; Maisel et al., meta-analysis of naltrexone and acamprosate (Tier B, item 68; not read).

Jonas et al., systematic review and meta-analysis of pharmacotherapy for alcohol use disorders in outpatient settings (alcohol list Tier A, item 29; not read for this card); claims should check its overlap with this review.
Palpacuer et al., systematic review of published and unpublished double-blind nalmefene trials, listed on the alcohol list as a critique of ESENSE 1 (Tier B, item 71; not read).
McPheeters et al., update of Jonas et al. (alcohol list Tier A, item 30; not read for this card).

replication.where_it_stands: This review pooled the double-blind naltrexone and nalmefene trials available to January 2010 and supports a modest add-on reduction in return to heavy drinking and drinking frequency at the end of treatment, with no clear effect on continuous abstinence, in detoxified treatment-seeking outpatients. Its nalmefene evidence (3 small trials, 396 participants) predates the larger trials it lists as ongoing, and its injectable evidence rests on 2 to 4 trials. The contrast often drawn between naltrexone for heavy drinking and acamprosate for abstinence is not shown by the three direct comparisons here, which found no difference between the two drugs on any drinking outcome. Later reviews on the alcohol list (Jonas et al., 2014; McPheeters et al., 2023) cover the same question with later trials; claims must not count trials shared between those reviews and this one as independent support. The PMC page shows no correction or later version; whether the Cochrane Library holds a newer version was not checked in this session.

funding.funder: Federal Ministry of Education and Research (BMBF), Germany, grant 01KG0724 (financial support and salary); internal support from Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich, Technical University of Munich and Chiang Mai University (infrastructure). The acknowledgements state that responsibility for the content remains with the authors.
funding.declared_conflicts: Rösner, Hackl-Herrwerth, Vecchi and Srisurapanont: no conflict of interest known. Leucht: speaker, consultancy or advisory board honoraria from SanofiAventis, BMS, EliLilly, Janssen/Johnson and Johnson, Lundbeck and Pfizer. Soyka: speaker, consultancy or advisory board honoraria from Lipha Pharmaceuticals, Forest Laboratories, Sanofi-Aventis, Essex Pharma, Eli Lilly, Prempharm and AstraZeneca.
funding.affiliations_note: Within this review, Lundbeck is the sponsor of the two ongoing nalmefene trials listed, and Lipha Pharmaceuticals donated study medication and placebo to, and monitored the sites of, the included COMBINE trial. Three authors (Rösner, Leucht, Soyka) wrote the earlier naltrexone and acamprosate meta-analysis cited as agreeing with this one, and Srisurapanont co-wrote the earlier versions of this review. Among the 50 trials, the study tables record industry funding or support for 12 (the text names 11; Anton 2004, funded by BioTie Therapies, is missing from its list). These are flags for closer reading, not reasons to discount.

what_would_settle_it: Large, registered, double-blind trials in people with alcohol use disorder recruited from ordinary care, including people with psychiatric comorbidity or other drug use and people still drinking, comparing naltrexone (including injectable and as-needed regimens) with placebo and with acamprosate, with prespecified primary outcomes, intention-to-treat analysis with principled handling of missing drinking data, biomarker-checked drinking, systematic adverse-event recording and at least 12 months of follow-up after treatment; and an individual-participant-data meta-analysis of the existing trials to explain the large between-trial heterogeneity.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population (DSM or ICD alcohol dependence), interventions (opioid antagonists alone or combined), comparators (placebo or active control) and outcomes are specified.

Cochrane protocol published in 1999 before the first version; deviations are listed with reasons in the differences between protocol and review. The re-selection of outcomes during data extraction according to availability is justified but was data-informed, and the funding sensitivity analysis and Egger test were added after the protocol.
Only double-blind randomised trials were eligible, without a stated reason for that choice (a reason is given only for the washout condition on crossover designs).

Four databases with strategies in Appendix 1, no language or date limits, four trial and results registers, investigators, experts and manufacturers contacted, reference lists searched, an unpublished dissertation and a congress abstract included; search in January 2010, within 24 months of publication.
Eligibility was assessed by one author, with a second consulted only in case of uncertainty (Methods › Selection of studies).
Outcome statistics were coded by two authors in parallel and independently and compared value by value; study characteristics were extracted by one author and checked by a second.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: 44 excluded full texts are listed with reasons (Characteristics of excluded studies). One reason differs between the text and the table (Karhuvaara 2007).

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Design, setting, country, diagnosis, required abstinence, baseline characteristics, interventions with doses, psychosocial treatment, outcomes with heavy-drinking definitions, funding, adherence and drop-out are tabulated for each trial.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: Cochrane 2008 tool with criteria in Appendix 3 (sequence generation, allocation concealment, blinding for all and subjective outcomes, incomplete binary and continuous data, selective reporting, baseline equivalence, objective validity checks), with support for each judgment; rated by one author and checked by a second. The card follows these judgments for the trials, which were not read.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: A financial-support row is given for every included trial.

Random-effects pooling with appropriate weighting was used and the choice was justified by reference, but the item also requires investigation of the causes of heterogeneity, and the review explicitly deferred its planned meta-regression to a later version although I2 was 61 to 94% for the continuous outcomes and heavy drinking was defined differently across trials; only an injectable-formulation subgroup and a funding comparison were run. Two analyses switched to fixed-effect models without explanation (post-treatment any drinking; injectable drinking days). This is the decisive item: a reader who counts the random-effects pooling as sufficient would rate the review moderate instead of low.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: No sensitivity analysis by risk-of-bias domain (for example excluding trials with inadequately handled missing data or unclear concealment); the funding and outcome-selection analyses address other questions.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The quality-of-evidence section discusses poorly reported randomisation, concealment and missing-data handling and notes that unclear concealment is associated with bias; met minimally, because the same section calls the evidence of high methodological quality and the conclusions carry no caveat.
I2 and tau-squared are reported and heterogeneity is called high, but its sources were not investigated (meta-regression postponed); the discussion only states that models are needed to explore it.

Funnel plot and Egger's regression test, discussed in the quality-of-evidence section. Weakly reported: the outcome tested and the number of trials (29) do not match the pooled analyses (see reporting issues), and the slight asymmetry seen in the funnel plot is not weighed.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Funding and each author's declarations are reported.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: One critical item is not met (11: the causes of large heterogeneity were not investigated, the planned meta-regression having been deferred, and two analyses switched to fixed-effect models without explanation), which under AMSTAR 2 gives low confidence; critical items 2, 4, 7, 9, 13 and 15 are met, 13 and 15 only minimally. Non-critical weaknesses: no reason given for restricting to double-blind trials (3), single-author study selection (5), no analysis of the impact of risk of bias (12) and heterogeneity not explained (14). The rating concerns how far the pooled numbers can be trusted as summaries; it is not a judgment of the trials, for which the card follows the review's own Cochrane appraisal (allocation concealment adequate in 3 of 50 trials, sequence generation in 14, missing binary data handled adequately in 11 of 40). The review may be cited for the end-of-treatment estimates of oral naltrexone against placebo with their intervals (return to heavy drinking, drinking and heavy drinking days, amount per drinking day, GGT), for the absence of a clear effect on return to any drinking, and for the side-effect and drop-out estimates; not for nalmefene, injectable naltrexone, head-to-head or combination comparisons beyond saying that the trials were too few to tell, and not for the claim that naltrexone supports abstinence.

key_findings.finding: The search found 681 records (621 from databases, 60 from other sources); after 463 duplicates, 218 were screened, 94 full texts assessed and 44 excluded. 50 double-blind RCTs were included: 47 of naltrexone and 3 of nalmefene, 7793 participants (3881 given naltrexone, 286 nalmefene, 3626 placebo or an active control).
key_findings.locator: Results › Description of studies › Results of the search; Included studies, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Return to heavy drinking (in most trials 5 or more standard drinks on a drinking day or occasion for men, 4 for women), naltrexone against placebo at the end of treatment: RR 0.83 (95% CI 0.76 to 0.90), 28 trials, 4433 participants, random effects; NNTB 9.09 (6.66 to 14.28); tau-squared 0.02.
key_findings.locator: Results › Effects of interventions › 01 Naltrexone versus placebo › Treatment phase, 1st paragraph; Results › Effects of interventions › Heterogeneity; Data and analyses, Comparison 1, outcome 1
key_findings.note: Editors' calculations: the NNTB corresponds to a risk difference of about 0.11 (0.07 to 0.15); an approximate 95% prediction interval from the printed tau-squared is RR 0.61 to 1.12. The discussion gives the NNTB's lower limit as 6.67.

key_findings.finding: Return to any drinking (the complement of continuous abstinence): RR 0.96 (0.92 to 1.00), 27 trials, 4693 participants, I2 28%, random effects; with a fixed-effect model RR 0.95 (0.92 to 0.98), which the authors say makes the conclusion on this outcome depend on the model chosen.
key_findings.locator: Results › Effects of interventions › 01 Naltrexone versus placebo › Treatment phase, 1st paragraph; Sensitivity analyses, 1st paragraph; Data and analyses, Comparison 1, outcomes 2 and 58
key_findings.note: The discussion prints the random-effects upper limit as 1.01.

key_findings.finding: Drinking frequency and amount: drinking days MD -3.89 percentage points (-5.75 to -2.04), 26 trials, 3882 participants, I2 94%, tau-squared 9.59; heavy drinking days MD -3.25 (-5.51 to -0.99), 15 trials, 1715, I2 81%, tau-squared 10.71; alcohol per drinking day MD -10.83 g (-19.69 to -1.97), 16 trials, 1838, I2 66%; GGT MD -10.37 U/L (-18.99 to -1.75), 16 trials, 1645, I2 61%. The authors translate these into about one fewer heavy-drinking day a month and about one drink less per drinking day.
key_findings.locator: Results › Effects of interventions › 01 Naltrexone versus placebo › Treatment phase, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Results › Effects of interventions › Heterogeneity; Data and analyses, Comparison 1, outcomes 3 to 6; Authors' conclusions › Implications for practice, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Editors' approximate 95% prediction intervals: drinking days -10.6 to 2.8 percentage points; heavy drinking days -10.7 to 4.2. Grams were converted from standard drinks with trial or ICAP 2003 country values.

key_findings.finding: Side effects, naltrexone against placebo (risk differences): any side effect 0.05 (0.01 to 0.09), 9 trials, 1021. Of 45 side effects pooled, 16 were more frequent on naltrexone, among them nausea 0.10 (0.07 to 0.13; 25 trials, 4334), daytime sleepiness 0.09 (0.05 to 0.14; 12 trials, 2802), dizziness 0.06 (0.04 to 0.08; 16 trials, 2655), abdominal pain 0.08 (0.04 to 0.11; 13 trials), decreased appetite 0.07 (0.03 to 0.11; 12 trials), vomiting 0.07 (0.04 to 0.09; 14 trials), somnolence 0.10 (0.05 to 0.14; 5 trials), drowsiness 0.10 (0.00 to 0.19; 5 trials), fatigue 0.05 (0.01 to 0.09), insomnia 0.03 (0.00 to 0.06), depression 0.04 (0.00 to 0.08), nightmares 0.10 (0.04 to 0.16), blurred vision 0.13 (0.04 to 0.21), decreased libido 0.08 (0.01 to 0.16), lethargy 0.13 (0.04 to 0.23) and weakness 0.17 (0.05 to 0.29), the last four from 2 or 3 trials. Headache did not differ (0.01, -0.02 to 0.04; 22 trials, 3633).
key_findings.locator: Results › Effects of interventions › 01 Naltrexone versus placebo › Treatment phase, 3rd paragraph; Data and analyses, Comparison 1, outcomes 7 to 53

key_findings.finding: Serious adverse events did not increase: RD -0.02 (-0.05 to 0.00), 9 trials, 1526 participants. Drop-out because of adverse events was more frequent on naltrexone: RR 1.60 (1.15 to 2.23), 22 trials, 3393. Drop-out for any reason: RR 0.92 (0.83 to 1.01), 37 trials, 5572. The discussion states that adverse events led one in 50 patients to stop naltrexone.
key_findings.locator: Results › Effects of interventions › 01 Naltrexone versus placebo › Treatment phase, 3rd paragraph; Discussion › Summary of main results, 3rd paragraph; Data and analyses, Comparison 1, outcomes 46, 54 and 55
key_findings.note: The data table prints the serious-adverse-event upper limit as -0.00. The one-in-50 figure is not derived anywhere in the review.

key_findings.finding: After treatment ended (3 to 12 months later, per the text): return to heavy drinking RR 0.86 (0.75 to 0.99), 5 trials, 1061 participants; return to any drinking RR 0.94 (0.79 to 1.11), 2 trials, 185 (fixed-effect model).
key_findings.locator: Results › Effects of interventions › 01 Naltrexone versus placebo › Post-treatment results; Data and analyses, Comparison 1, outcomes 56 and 57
key_findings.note: Post-treatment follow-up in the included trials ranged from 3 to 17 months (Results › Included studies); the discussion says six trials provided post-treatment data.

key_findings.finding: By funding source: industry-sponsored trials RR 0.90 (0.78 to 1.05), 7 trials, 1121 participants; non-profit trials RR 0.84 (0.77 to 0.91), 19 trials, 3125; overall 0.86 (0.79 to 0.92), 26 trials, 4246. The abstract reports no significant difference.
key_findings.locator: Results › Effects of interventions › 01 Naltrexone versus placebo › Sensitivity analyses, 2nd paragraph; Data and analyses, Comparison 1, outcome 59
key_findings.note: The outcome analysed is uncertain (see reporting issues). Editors' z-test of the two subgroup estimates: p of about 0.43, with low power.

key_findings.finding: In an analysis shown only in the data table, return to any drinking from published results (20 trials, 2917 participants) gave RR 0.94 (0.90 to 1.00), and from results supplied later by investigators (7 trials, 1776) RR 0.98 (0.92 to 1.04).
key_findings.locator: Data and analyses, Comparison 1, outcome 60 (60.1 and 60.2)
key_findings.note: Editors' z-test of the difference: p of about 0.31. The review does not describe or discuss this analysis.

key_findings.finding: Publication bias: the funnel plot showed slight asymmetry with a gap at the bottom; Egger's regression test was not significant, unweighted (R2 0.20, P = 0.229, SE 1.440, n = 29) or weighted (R2 0.52, P = 0.765, SE 1.221, n = 29).
key_findings.locator: Results › Risk of bias in included studies › Other potential sources of bias, paragraph headed Publication bias; Figure 4 legend
key_findings.note: The outcome tested is inconsistent between methods and figure legend, and n = 29 matches neither primary pool (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Risk of bias of the trials, review's judgments: sequence generation adequately described in 14 of 50; allocation concealment adequate in 3 of 50; blinding adequate in 21, with integrity tested and confirmed in 6; objective checks of self-reported drinking in 30 to 31; missing binary data handled adequately in 11 of 40 trials with binary outcomes, inadequately in 4 and unclearly in 25; missing continuous data adequate in 12 of 26 trials reporting drinking days and inadequate in 5; selective reporting low risk in 48 of 50.
key_findings.locator: Results › Risk of bias in included studies › Allocation; Blinding; Incomplete outcome data; Selective reporting; Other potential sources of bias

key_findings.finding: Extended-release injectable naltrexone against placebo (subgroup of Garbutt 2005, Johnson 2004, Kranzler 1998, Kranzler 2004): return to any drinking RR 0.92 (0.84 to 1.00), 2 trials, 486; drinking days MD -8.54 (-15.77 to -1.31), 2 trials, 335, fixed effect; heavy drinking days MD -3.05 (-8.46 to 2.35), 3 trials, 357; more daytime sleepiness (RD 0.22, 0.02 to 0.42; 2 trials, 50 participants), decreased appetite (0.08), dizziness (0.08), fatigue (0.06) and vomiting (0.06); drop-out due to adverse events RR 1.57 (0.92 to 2.69), 3 trials, 969.
key_findings.locator: Results › Effects of interventions › 02 Subgroup analyses: Injectable naltrexone, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Data and analyses, Comparison 2

key_findings.finding: Naltrexone against acamprosate (Anton 2006, Kiefer 2003, Morley 2006): return to heavy drinking RR 0.96 (0.87 to 1.06) and to any drinking 0.97 (0.91 to 1.04), 3 trials, 800 participants; drinking days MD 2.98 (-7.45 to 13.42), 2 trials, 720; more nausea (RD 0.08, 0.03 to 0.13) and somnolence (0.07, 0.01 to 0.13) on naltrexone and more diarrhoea on acamprosate (RD -0.27, -0.34 to -0.20); drop-out due to adverse events RR 1.31 (0.63 to 2.73).
key_findings.locator: Results › Effects of interventions › 03 Naltrexone versus acamprosate, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Data and analyses, Comparison 3
key_findings.note: The text gives drinking days as MD 3.06 (-7.42 to 13.53) from three trials; the table values are used here.

key_findings.finding: Naltrexone plus acamprosate (Anton 2006, Kiefer 2003; 694 participants): against placebo, return to heavy drinking RR 0.71 (0.38 to 1.35) and to any drinking 0.70 (0.35 to 1.39), more diarrhoea (RD 0.20, 0.13 to 0.27) and nausea (0.20, 0.14 to 0.26), drop-out due to adverse events RR 3.75 (1.33 to 10.55); against naltrexone alone, return to heavy drinking 0.97 (0.75 to 1.26) and to any drinking 0.88 (0.61 to 1.28), more diarrhoea (RD 0.37, 0.10 to 0.65) and nausea (0.09, 0.02 to 0.16).
key_findings.locator: Results › Effects of interventions › Naltrexone + acamprosate versus placebo; Naltrexone + acamprosate versus naltrexone; Data and analyses, Comparisons 4 and 5

key_findings.finding: Nalmefene against placebo (Anton 2004, Mason 1994, Mason 1999; 396 participants): return to heavy drinking RR 0.85 (0.67 to 1.08); alcohol per drinking day MD -4.16 g (-32.69 to 24.37), 2 trials, 126; more insomnia (RD 0.12, 0.05 to 0.19); drop-out due to adverse events RR 1.43 (0.22 to 9.24); drop-out RR 0.92 (0.68 to 1.25). None of the efficacy results was significant.
key_findings.locator: Results › Effects of interventions › Nalmefene versus placebo › Treatment phase, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Data and analyses, Comparison 6
key_findings.note: The text also gives return to any drinking RR 0.92 (0.70 to 1.20), heavy drinking days MD -4.70 (-12.38 to 2.98) and dizziness RD 0.15 (0.05 to 0.25), none of which is in the data table; the nausea row is unusable (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Single-trial comparisons of naltrexone with aripiprazole (Martinotti 2008), nefazodone (Kranzler 2000) and topiramate (Baltieri 2008) showed no significant differences on drinking outcomes, with point estimates favouring the comparators (for example return to any drinking against topiramate RR 1.33, 0.98 to 1.80; drinking days MD 13.30, -2.01 to 28.61).
key_findings.locator: Results › Effects of interventions › 04 Naltrexone versus apripiprazole, nefazodone or topiramate, 1st to 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: The review's estimate is smaller than in the 2005 version, which gave RR 0.64 (0.51 to 0.82) for return to heavy drinking (7 trials, 822 patients) and 0.91 (0.81 to 1.02) for any drinking (10 trials, 1014); the authors attribute the change to newer trials with negative results.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Agreements and disagreements with other studies or reviews

key_findings.finding: Outcome completeness: the primary outcomes were available from 28 (56%), 27 (54%) and 26 (52%) of the 50 trials, alcohol amount and GGT from 16 (32%), heavy drinking days from 15 (30%) and post-treatment results from 6 (12%). Applicability: almost all participants were detoxified, oral naltrexone was nearly always 50 mg a day, treatment was outpatient, and people with psychiatric diagnoses were screened out of most trials.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Overall completeness and applicability of evidence › Completeness of the database; Applicability of the results

reporting_issues.issue: The nalmefene nausea result (Comparison 6, outcome 4) gives 2 trials with 694 participants and RD 0.20 (0.14 to 0.26), identical to the naltrexone-plus-acamprosate against placebo nausea row (Comparison 4, outcome 4); the three nalmefene trials have 396 participants in all. The results text repeats RD 0.20 for nalmefene.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Data and analyses, Comparisons 4 and 6; Results › Effects of interventions › Nalmefene versus placebo, 2nd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The nalmefene nausea estimate appears to have been copied from another comparison and must not be cited.

reporting_issues.issue: The methods state that the sensitivity analysis by funding source was run on return to any drinking, but Analysis 1.59 has 26 trials and 4246 participants, matching neither the 27-trial any-drinking pool nor the 28-trial heavy-drinking pool, and its overall RR 0.86 (0.79 to 0.92) and subgroup estimates (0.84 and 0.90) cannot come from the any-drinking data (pooled RR 0.96); the figure legend labels it outcome 1.93. The industry subgroup holds 7 trials, although 11 trials are called industry-sponsored. No test for subgroup difference is reported.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methods › Sensitivity analysis; Results › Effects of interventions › 01 › Sensitivity analyses, 2nd paragraph; Data and analyses, Comparison 1, outcome 59; Figure 11 legend
reporting_issues.consequence: The outcome on which industry and non-profit trials were compared is unclear (it resembles return to heavy drinking); the abstract's statement that the two did not differ should be cited with that uncertainty and with the low power of the comparison (editors' z-test p of about 0.43).

reporting_issues.issue: The methods specify Egger's test on the log odds ratio for return to any drinking; the funnel plot legend names outcome 1.1, return to heavy drinking; the test reports n = 29 trials, while the pooled analyses have 27 (any drinking) and 28 (heavy drinking) trials.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methods › Assessment of reporting biases; Results › Risk of bias in included studies › Other potential sources of bias (Publication bias); Figure 4 legend; Data and analyses, Comparison 1
reporting_issues.consequence: Which data set was tested is unclear; the abstract's P = 0.765 (the weighted test; unweighted P = 0.229) should not be read as clearing the pooled estimates of small-study effects, particularly as the funnel plot showed slight asymmetry. The unweighted test's standard error (1.440) and the wording describing the funnel plot are identical in the companion acamprosate review (card sc_rosner_2010b), which tested a different set of trials.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract and the summary of main results say effects of injectable naltrexone missed statistical significance, but its drinking-days result is significant (MD -8.54, -15.77 to -1.31; 2 trials, 335 participants), from a fixed-effect model, while the methods state random effects throughout; post-treatment return to any drinking also uses a fixed-effect model.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Abstract › Main results; Discussion › Summary of main results, 4th paragraph; Data and analyses, Comparison 2, outcome 2; Comparison 1, outcome 57
reporting_issues.consequence: The injectable results are mixed rather than uniformly non-significant, and the significant one depends on an unexplained fixed-effect choice; claims should cite the three injectable estimates separately with their trial counts.

reporting_issues.issue: Text and data table disagree for some numbers: naltrexone against acamprosate drinking days is MD 3.06 (-7.42 to 13.53) from three trials in the text and 2.98 (-7.45 to 13.42) from two in the table; naltrexone plus acamprosate against naltrexone drop-out is RR 1.03 (0.95 to 1.43) in the text, an interval that is not symmetric around the estimate on the log scale, and 1.03 (0.72 to 1.48) in the table; the any-drinking upper limit is 1.00 in the abstract and results and 1.01 in the discussion; the NNTB lower limit is 6.66 and 6.67.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Effects of interventions › 03 and Naltrexone + acamprosate versus naltrexone; Discussion › Agreements and disagreements; Data and analyses, Comparisons 3 and 5

reporting_issues.issue: The paragraph on naltrexone combined with ondansetron or sertraline says both combinations significantly reduced drinking days, but the ondansetron trial's MD -23.80 (-58.13 to 10.53) crosses zero; the sertraline trial's amount per drinking day is described as about 28 g but printed with the drinking-days numbers (MD -10.6, -12.06 to -9.14); its GGT interval lacks the minus sign on the lower limit (33.79 to 19.19); and its side effects are labelled RR with values (0.40, 0.29, 0.25) that read as risk differences, attributed to sertraline although the arm was naltrexone plus sertraline. None of these results is in the data table.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Effects of interventions › Naltrexone + ondansetrone / sertraline versus placebo
reporting_issues.consequence: These single-trial combination results cannot be checked and should not be cited from this review.

reporting_issues.issue: Results given in the text but absent from the data table: nalmefene return to any drinking, heavy drinking days and dizziness; naltrexone plus acamprosate against placebo drinking days, GGT, decreased appetite and vomiting; naltrexone plus acamprosate against naltrexone drinking days and GGT (MD 10.7, 1.87 to 19.93, an interval centred on 10.9 by the editors' arithmetic); all outcomes of naltrexone against aripiprazole, nefazodone and topiramate. Conversely, the outcome-selection analysis (Comparison 1, outcome 60) is in the table but described nowhere in the text.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Effects of interventions; Data and analyses, Comparisons 1 and 4 to 6
reporting_issues.consequence: Text-only numbers cannot be checked against a pooled analysis; the unreported outcome-selection analysis, in which investigator-supplied results showed a smaller effect than published ones, is relevant to reporting bias but is not discussed.

reporting_issues.issue: Descriptive counts do not add up: funding categories sum to 54 trials (11 industry, 4 no information, 39 non-profit) and countries to 54 (37 USA, 8 Europe, 3 each for Australia, Asia and Latin America); 48 trials are said to have excluded psychiatric comorbidity while 6 others did not; outcome availability is 32, 29 and 28 trials for the primary outcomes in the results but 28, 27 and 26 in the discussion and data table; a placebo run-in is attributed to seven trials while eight are named. By the editors' tally of the study tables, 12 trials had industry funding or support (Anton 2004, funded by BioTie Therapies, is missing from the text's list), 4 gave no information and 34 were non-profit; 32 trials were in the USA and 9 in Europe (Martinotti 2008, Italy, is missing from the text's list).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Description of studies › Included studies (Patients; Treatment setting and study design; Outcomes); Discussion › Completeness of the database; Characteristics of included studies
reporting_issues.consequence: Descriptive counts should be taken from the study tables (editors' tally), not from the text; the funding count matters for any claim about industry sponsorship.

reporting_issues.issue: Smaller slips: Kranzler 2000 is described once as comparing naltrexone with a serotonin-antagonist nalmefene, but its study table and the later results describe nefazodone; Karhuvaara 2007 is excluded for targeted treatment in the text and for a sample of heavy drinkers in the excluded-studies table; the minimum treatment duration is four weeks in the inclusion criteria and 30 days in the exclusions paragraph; dyspepsia (RD -0.06, -0.11 to -0.00) is counted among the non-significant side effects although its interval lies just below zero.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Description of studies › Included studies (Comparisons) and Excluded studies; Methods › Types of interventions; Data and analyses, Comparison 1, outcome 24
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; they affect auditing of the review rather than its main estimates.

verification.first_pass_by: AI (Claude, reading agent), AI reader 161 (first reader)
verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC13590218 (Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews 2010, Issue 12, CD001867, version pub3, dated 8 December 2010 on the page; its DOI 10.1002/14651858.CD001867.pub3 matches the assigned DOI): abstract, plain language summary, all sections, the Data and analyses summary tables (rendered as text), the characteristics of included, excluded and ongoing studies with the trial-level risk-of-bias tables, Appendices 1 to 3, what's new, history, acknowledgements, differences between protocol and review, contributions of authors, sources of support, declarations of interest and the reference list. The PRISMA flow diagram, the risk-of-bias graph and summary, the funnel plot and all forest plots are images and their values were not extracted. No supplementary files. The page links no correction notice; the included trials were not read.
